statements.claim: Of all the doors Krishna knocked on during his peace mission to Hastinapura, the hardest was Duryodhana's; Bhishma and Drona had listened and Vidura needed no persuading.
statements.evidence: Mission recap consistent with prior corpus events (DKS_0426-0428) and 5.124, where Dhritarashtra names Bhishma, Vidura and friends who seek Duryodhana's good.

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra found everything Krishna said true, reasonable, and good for the world, but lacked the resolve to act.
statements.evidence: 5.124: "Thou hast... told me that which leadeth to heaven, what is beneficial to the world, consistent with virtue, and fraught with reason. I am not, however, independent."

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra confesses he is not independent: Duryodhana never does what pleases him and heeds neither Gandhari, Vidura, nor friends headed by Bhishma; he asks Krishna to counsel the crooked, senseless prince.
statements.evidence: 5.124 Dhritarashtra speech reproduced nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: Krishna stood before the ever-wrathful Duryodhana and spoke sweet words meant for his good and that of his followers.
statements.evidence: 5.124: Krishna "approached nearer to the ever-wrathful Duryodhana and said unto him these sweet words... uttered especially for thy good, as also... for that of thy followers."

statements.claim: Krishna's opening counsel: Duryodhana is born in a race distinguished for wisdom, should act righteously; only the wicked-souled, cruel and shameless act as he does; persistence in such behaviour is sinful, frightful, capable of leading to death, causeless and unsustainable.
statements.evidence: 5.124 Krishna speech matches passage almost verbatim.

statements.claim: If Duryodhana avoided what is productive only of woe he would escape the sinful deeds of his brothers, followers and counsellors; Krishna urges peace with the wise, brave, learned sons of Pandu whose souls are under control.
statements.evidence: 5.124: "If by avoiding this which is productive only of woe... thou wilt escape from the sinful and disreputable deeds of thy brothers, followers, and counsellors. Then... make peace... with the sons of Pandu..."

statements.claim: Such peace would please Dhritarashtra, Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, Somadatta, Vahlika, Ashwatthama, Vikarna, Sanjaya, Vivinsati and many kinsmen; the whole world would benefit.
statements.evidence: 5.124 list matches the passage exactly.

statements.claim: Krishna urges obedience to father and mother, citing the Kimpaka simile, the ruin of those who reject beneficial counsel, and the happiness of those who accept it at once.
statements.evidence: 5.124 contains all three counsels.

statements.claim: He who rejects well-meaning friends is soon subjugated by foes; the companion of the sinful who honours strangers but hates his own is cast off by the Earth; Duryodhana has quarrelled with kin and seeks protection from the sinful and foolish.
statements.evidence: 5.124 closing counsel matches passage (pack excerpt truncates at "What other man is there on earth bes...").

statements.claim: Scene closes with Krishna falling silent while the Kuru court holds its breath.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric close; adds no sourceable fact.

notes: Speech quotes track Ganguli 5.124 closely (incl. kinsmen list and Kimpaka simile). No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Duryodhana rose to answer Krishna's counsel in the Kuru assembly.
statements.evidence: 5.127 opens: "Hearing in that assembly of the Kurus these words that were disagreeable to him, Duryodhana replied unto the mighty-armed Kesava."

statements.claim: Duryodhana: "It behooves you, O Kesava, to speak after reflecting on all circumstances"; he finds no fault in himself, not even a minute one, while Krishna, Vidura, the king, the preceptor and the grandsire blame only him.
statements.evidence: 5.127: "It behoveth thee, O Kesava, to speak after reflecting on all circumstances... I do not, even after reflection, behold any grave fault in me, or even... any fault however minute."

statements.claim: In the dice game joyfully accepted by the Pandavas, they were vanquished and Shakuni won their kingdom; Duryodhana ordered the won wealth returned; their second defeat and exile to the woods was no fault of the Kauravas.
statements.evidence: 5.127: "the Pandavas were vanquished and their kingdom was won by Sakuni... the wealth that was won from the Pandavas then, was ordered by me, to be returned unto them."

statements.claim: The Pandavas, though really weak, cheerfully seek a quarrel as if strong; Duryodhana asks what they have done to them.
statements.evidence: 5.127: "though (really) weak, why do the Pandavas yet so cheerfully seek a quarrel with us, as if they were strong? What have we done to them?"

statements.claim: The Kauravas will not bow down in fear, not even to Indra; the gods themselves cannot vanquish Bhishma, Kripa, Drona and Karna in battle.
statements.evidence: 5.127: "We cannot bow down to Indra himself, let alone the sons of Pandu... the very gods are not competent to vanquish Bhishma, Kripa, Drona and Karna, in battle."

statements.claim: Falling on a bed of arrows in battle is the Kshatriya's highest duty and leads to heaven; none nobly born would bow to an enemy from fear of death.
statements.evidence: 5.127: "even this is our highest duty as Kshatriyas, viz., that we should lay ourselves down on the field of battle on a bed of arrows."

statements.claim: Duryodhana invokes Matanga's saying: a Kshatriya should keep erect and never bow, should break at the knots rather than bend, and bows only to Brahmanas for piety.
statements.evidence: 5.127: "accept regardfully this saying of Matanga... one should always keep himself erect, and never bow down... one should rather break at the knots than bend."

statements.claim: The share of the kingdom formerly given by his father shall never again be obtainable by the Pandavas as long as he lives; both sides should live in dependence on Dhritarashtra; the kingdom was given away from ignorance or fear when he was a child.
statements.evidence: 5.127: "That share in the kingdom which was formerly given them by my father shall never again... be obtainable by them as long as I live. As long... as king Dhritarashtra liveth, both ourselves and they... should live in dependence on him."

statements.claim: Not even land covered by the point of a sharp needle shall be given to the Pandavas as long as Duryodhana lives.
statements.evidence: 5.127: "even that much of our land which may be covered by the point of a sharp needle shall not... be given by us unto the Pandavas."

statements.claim: The peace mission had asked for five villages, a token, anything to avoid war.
statements.evidence: Recap of the corpus-established five-village request (DKS_0409/0410/0419; Draupadi names Avishthala, Vrikasthala, Makandi, Varanavata and a fifth). Not in pack 5.127 but consistent with the corpus chain and not contradicted.

notes: Reply speech is a faithful condensation of Ganguli 5.127; no unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Krishna reflected with eyes red in anger before answering; the sweet counsel of the morning was gone.
statements.evidence: 5.128: "Reflecting (for a moment), with eyes red in anger, he, of Dasarha's race... said these words."

statements.claim: "Wishest thou for a bed of heroes? Verily, thou shalt have it, with thy counsellors. Wait but a short while — a great slaughter will ensue."
statements.evidence: 5.128 quoted verbatim.

statements.claim: Krishna charges that Duryodhana, grieved at the Pandavas' prosperity, conspired with Suvala's son about the gambling match, without consulting righteous persons.
statements.evidence: 5.128: "Grieved at the prosperity of the high-souled Pandavas, thou conspirest... with Suvala's son about the gambling match... It was thou who hadst devised... without consulting with persons of righteous behaviour."

statements.claim: Gambling robs even the good of understanding and brings disunion and dire consequence to the wicked.
statements.evidence: 5.128: "gambling robs even the good of their understanding, and as regards the wicked, disunion and dire consequence spring from it."

statements.claim: Krishna recalls Duryodhana's insult of Draupadi — dragging a brother's wife into the assembly — and the heartless language used by Karna, Dussasana and Duryodhana to the sons of Kunti as they set out for the woods.
statements.evidence: 5.128: "Who else is there, capable of insulting a brother's wife in the way thou didst or of dragging her into the assembly..." and "Language such as becomes only those that are heartless and despicable, was frequently repeated by Karna and Dussasana and also by thee."

statements.claim: Krishna recounts the attempt to burn the Pandavas with their mother at Varanavata while they were children, their concealment at Ekachakra in a brahmana's abode, and Duryodhana's poison, snake and cord attempts — all unsuccessful.
statements.evidence: 5.128: "Thou hadst taken great pains to burn to death, at Varanavata, the sons of Pandu with their mother... After this... they were obliged to live for a long while, concealed in the town of Ekachakra in the abode of a Brahmana. With poison, with snakes and cords..."

statements.claim: Krishna prophesies Duryodhana must yield the paternal share when, divested of prosperity, he is laid low, and chides him for seeking to appear in a different garb despite innumerable wrongs.
statements.evidence: 5.128: "Thou art not... willing to give them their paternal share... Thou shalt have to give it them, this, when divested of prosperity, thou shalt be laid low."

statements.claim: Krishna notes Duryodhana ignores repeated pleas for peace from his parents, Bhishma, Drona and Vidura; peace does not recommend itself to him through loss of understanding; the act he is about to do is sinful and disreputable.
statements.evidence: 5.128: "Though repeatedly solicited by thy parents, by Bhishma, Drona, and Vidura, to make peace, thou dost not yet... make peace... Sinful and disreputable is that act, which thou... art about to do."

statements.claim: Dussasana rises and warns that if Duryodhana will not make peace, the Kauravas will bind him and hand him to the son of Kunti; Bhishma, Drona and his father will give over Vikartana's son (Karna), Duryodhana and Dussasana to the Pandavas.
statements.evidence: 5.128 Dussasana's interjection quoted nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: Duryodhana, breathing heavily like a great snake, rose in anger, disregarded Vidura, Dhritarashtra, Vahlika, Kripa, Somadatta, Bhishma, Drona and Krishna, and walked out; his brother, counsellors and the kings followed and the assembly emptied.
statements.evidence: 5.128: "Suyodhana, breathing heavily like a great snake rose up from his seat in anger, and disregarding Vidura, and Dhritarashtra... and Janardana, in fact, all of them, went out of the court... his brother and all his counsellors, and all the kings, followed him."

statements.claim: Bhishma laments that the enemies of one who follows wrath and avarice rejoice at his coming distress; the hour of all the Kshatriyas has arrived.
statements.evidence: 5.128 Bhishma's speech matches the passage.

notes: Rebuke, Dussasana interjection, exit and Bhishma's lament all track Ganguli 5.128; no unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: After Duryodhana and his followers left, Krishna stood before the remaining elders of the Kuru race.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.128): Krishna tells the elders of the Kuru race they are guilty of great transgression for not seizing the wicked king — delivered after Duryodhana's exit, per the story's framing.

statements.claim: "Even this is great transgression... of which all the elders of the Kuru race are becoming guilty — for they do not forcibly seize and bind this wicked king."
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.128) quotes this nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: The counsellors had watched Duryodhana refuse peace, insult a brother's wife, and plot murder by fire and poison, yet let him walk out; standing by was itself a crime in Krishna's telling.
statements.evidence: Recap of crimes detailed in the same section (5.127-5.128) and corpus chain; framing, not a new sourceable claim.

statements.claim: Krishna cites his own example: "Kansa, the son of Ugrasena, abandoned by his relatives, was slain by me in a great encounter, from desire of benefiting my kinsmen."
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.128) quotes this verbatim.

statements.claim: The old kings knew the Kamsa story: tyrant of Mathura who imprisoned his own sister and murdered her children, hunted his nephew, and was struck down by the kinsman he had wronged.
statements.evidence: Background lore covered earlier in the corpus (Kamsa arc, DKS_0005-0138) and consistent with the excerpt's "slain by me... from desire of benefiting my kinsmen"; not itself in pack 5.128.

statements.claim: "Binding Duryodhana fast... make peace with the Pandavas."
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.128): "binding Duryodhana fast, make peace with the Pandavas."

statements.claim: Krishna had come to Hastinapura asking for five villages and a chance for the cousins to live; he left the elders with the question of whether they would seize Duryodhana.
statements.evidence: Five-village request established earlier in the corpus (DKS_0409/0410/0419); remainder is narrative framing.

statements.claim: No elder stepped forward or laid a hand on the king, and Krishna had nothing left to say to men who would not act.
statements.evidence: Consistent with the pack: no seizure is recorded and 5.130 opens with Duryodhana free and plotting; the silence and finality are dramatic inference.

notes: Core indictment, Kansa citation and binding command all match the 5.128 excerpt. Kamsa background and five-villages recap are corpus-established, not flagged.

statements.claim: The conspiracy began when Duryodhana, deaf to the grave words his mother had just spoken to him, went away in anger to wicked men.
statements.evidence: 5.130: "Disregarding these words of grave import, spoken by his mother, Duryodhana went away, in anger, from that place to the presence of wicked persons."

statements.claim: Duryodhana consulted with Sakuni, Suvala's son, most clever in dice (who had once gambled away the Pandavas' kingdom); Karna and Dussasana joined, making four.
statements.evidence: 5.130: "the Kuru prince began to consult with Suvala's royal son, Sakuni, most clever in dice... Duryodhana and Karna and Suvala's son Sakuni, with Dussasana as their fourth."

statements.claim: The four resolved: "This Janardana, quick in action, seeks, with king Dhritarashtra and Bhishma the son of Santanu, to seize us first. We, however, shall forcibly seize this tiger among men, Hrishikesa... as Indra once forcibly seized Vali, the son of Virochana."
statements.evidence: 5.130 resolution quoted nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: They reasoned that with Krishna seized the Pandavas would lose heart like snakes with broken fangs; he was their refuge, the grantor of wishes, bull of the Satwatas; confined, the Pandavas with the Somakas would sit depressed; so, disregarding Dhritarashtra's cries, they would seize Kesava and fight.
statements.evidence: 5.130: all four arguments present in the passage.

statements.claim: Satyaki, capable of reading the heart by signs, came to know of the plot before the plotters had finished shaping it; the illustrative signs (glances, lowered voice, hand on sword hilt) are colour.
statements.evidence: 5.130: "highly intelligent Satyaki, capable of reading the heart by signs, soon came to know of it." (Specific gestures are atmospheric elaboration — connective.)

statements.claim: Satyaki left the court with Kritavarman, Hridika's son, ordered him to array mail-clad troops and wait at the court's entrance, then re-entered like a lion entering a mountain-cave.
statements.evidence: 5.130: Satyaki told Kritavarman, "Array the troops soon. And accoutred in mail... wait thou at the entrance of the court, till I represent this matter unto Krishna"... re-entered the court, like a lion entering a mountain-cave.

statements.claim: Satyaki informed Kesava first, then Dhritarashtra, then Vidura, and laughingly said the plotters were like idiots and children trying to seize a blazing fire with their garments.
statements.evidence: 5.130: "He (first) informed the high-souled Kesava and then Dhritarashtra, and then Vidura... he laughingly said... are like idiots and children desiring to seize a blazing fire by means of their garments."

statements.claim: Vidura warned Dhritarashtra that the hour of all his sons was come; united they desired to vanquish the younger brother of Vasava and would perish like insects in a blazing fire; Janardana could send them all to Yama's abode but would never deviate from virtue.
statements.evidence: 5.130 Vidura's speech matches the passage nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: Kritavarman's mail-clad ranks stood at the door while the man they meant to seize sat untouched in the hall.
statements.evidence: 5.130: Kritavarman posted arrayed, mail-clad troops at the court's entrance; Krishna remained in the court throughout.

statements.claim: The conspiracy was dead before it was ever allowed to move.
statements.evidence: Dramatic close to the story's own scope (the alarm in 5.130); the seizure is never carried out in the pack.

notes: Conspiracy, Satyaki's alarm and Vidura's warning all track Ganguli 5.130 closely; no unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Every eye turned to Krishna after Satyaki's warning; the plot of Duryodhana, Karna, Sakuni and Dussasana stood exposed and Krishna had heard of it without moving a muscle.
statements.evidence: 5.130: Satyaki informed Kesava, Dhritarashtra and Vidura of the conspiracy; Krishna then spoke, casting his eyes on Dhritarashtra.

statements.claim: The four who had resolved on the seizure stood in the open assembly before Krishna, their certainty wavering under the eyes of the whole court.
statements.evidence: 5.130 places the four AWAY from the court: Duryodhana went "wending away from the court" to consult with Sakuni, and after Krishna's speech Dhritarashtra orders Vidura, "Quickly bring here sinful Duryodhana..." — "Kshattri once more caused unwilling Duryodhana to enter the court." The conspirators were not in the hall during Krishna's defiance; DKS_0433's own ending also leaves them outside.

statements.claim: Krishna told Dhritarashtra that if the men wished to chastise him by violence they might try; he could chastise them all, but would not perpetrate any sinful and censurable act.
statements.evidence: 5.130: "O king, if these (men) desire to chastise me by using violence, permit them to chastise me... I dare chastise all of them together that are so excited with rage, I will not, however, perpetrate any sinful and censurable act."

statements.claim: Krishna said that coveting the Pandavas' possessions, Dhritarashtra's sons would lose their own; seizing these men he could this very day make them over to the sons of Pritha, but he would commit no censurable deed born of wrath; he gave permission to all the king's sons.
statements.evidence: 5.130 speech matches the passage nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: Krishna spoke as one who could end the dispute with a single motion and chose instead to withhold himself; the conspiracy had failed because it was impossible from the moment it was conceived.
statements.evidence: Interpretive framing consistent with the speech and with Vidura's warning in 5.130.

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra told Vidura to bring sinful, sovereignty-coveting Duryodhana with his friends, counsellors, brothers and followers, to make one more effort to bring him to the right path.
statements.evidence: 5.130: "Quickly bring here sinful Duryodhana, who is so covetous of sovereignty, with his friends, counsellors, brothers, and followers. I shall see if indeed, making one more effort I can bring him to the right path."

statements.claim: Vidura went out and caused the unwilling Duryodhana to enter the court, surrounded by Karna and Dussasana and the kings who followed him.
statements.evidence: 5.130: "Kshattri once more caused unwilling Duryodhana to enter the court with his brothers, and surrounded by the kings (that followed him)."

corrections.original_sentence: The four who had resolved on the seizure stood where they were, and for the first time their certainty appeared to waver.
corrections.suggested: The four who had resolved on the seizure were not in the court to hear it — they had gone away from the assembly to shape their plot in secret, and their certainty would first waver only later, when Vidura brought the unwilling Duryodhana back before Krishna.

corrections.original_sentence: What they had planned in whispers looked different in the open, under the eyes of the whole court.
corrections.suggested: What they had planned in whispers had been carried into the open by Satyaki's warning, under the eyes of the whole court.

notes: Krishna's defiance speech, Dhritarashtra's command and Duryodhana's re-entry are faithful to 5.130, but the opening staging places the four conspirators inside the assembly during Krishna's defiance; the pack has them away from the court plotting (Duryodhana "wending away from the court," later fetched by Vidura: "bring here"), and DKS_0433's own ending likewise leaves them outside. Single contradicted staging claim (one sentence + its dependent sentence).

statements.claim: Krishna told Duryodhana that from delusion he regarded Krishna as alone and sought to make him captive by violence; here were all the Pandavas, Vrishnis and Andhakas, all the Adityas, Rudras and Vasus with the great Rishis.
statements.evidence: 5.131: "From delusion, O Suyodhana, thou regardest me to be alone... Here, however, are all the Pandavas and all the Vrishnis and Andhakas. Here are all the Adityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus, with all the great Rishis."

statements.claim: Krishna, the slayer of hostile heroes, burst into loud laughter.
statements.evidence: 5.131: "Saying this Kesava, that slayer of hostile heroes burst out into a loud laughter."

statements.claim: As the laughing Sauri blazed, myriads of thumb-sized gods of lightning effulgence issued from his body; Brahman appeared on his forehead, Rudra on his breast, the regents of the world on his arms; from his mouth issued Agni, the Adityas, Sadhyas, Vasus, Aswins, Marutas, Indra and the Viswedevas; myriads of Yakshas, Gandharvas and Rakshasas also came forth.
statements.evidence: 5.131 cosmic details match the passage nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: From his arms issued Sankarshana and Dhananjaya; Arjuna stood on his right with bow, Balarama on his left with the plough; behind stood Bhima, Yudhishthira and the two sons of Madri; before him the Andhakas and Vrishnis with Pradyumna bearing upraised weapons.
statements.evidence: 5.131 matches (Rama = Balarama; Sankarshana and Dhananjaya are Balarama and Arjuna).

statements.claim: On his countless arms appeared the conch, discus, mace, bow Saranga, plough, javelin and Nandaka — every named weapon, shining and upraised; fierce sparks of fire mixed with smoke issued from eyes, nose, ears and every part, and sun-like sparks from the pores of his skin.
statements.evidence: 5.131 weapon list and fire details match verbatim.

statements.claim: All the kings closed their eyes with affrighted hearts except Drona, Bhishma, Vidura, greatly blessed Sanjaya and the ascetic Rishis, to whom Janardana gave divine sight.
statements.evidence: 5.131: "all the kings closed their eyes with affrighted hearts, except Drona, and Bhishma, and Vidura... greatly blessed Sanjaya, and the Rishis... for the divine Janardana gave unto them this divine sight on the occasion."

statements.claim: Celestial drums beat in the sky, a floral shower fell on him, the whole Earth trembled, the oceans were agitated and all the denizens of the earth were filled with wonder.
statements.evidence: 5.131 matches verbatim.

statements.claim: Krishna withdrew the divine, wonderful and auspicious form and was himself again, seated quietly in the assembly.
statements.evidence: 5.131: he withdrew the form and then "went out" arm-in-arm with Satyaki and Kritavarman (departure covered by DKS_0436); the brief seated pause is connective scene-timing, no contradiction.

statements.claim: The vision was the answer to the conspirators' boast — what the four had proposed to bind was the lord of the universe.
statements.evidence: Interpretive close consistent with Krishna's own words in 5.131.

notes: Universal-form description is an extremely faithful rendering of Ganguli 5.131; no unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: Krishna walked out of the Kuru court arm-in-arm with Satyaki and Kritavarman, Hridika's son, with the Rishis' permission; during the uproar the Rishis — Narada and others — vanished to their own places.
statements.evidence: 5.131: "arm-in-arm with Satyaki on one side and Hridika's son (Kritavarman) on the other, and obtaining permission of the Rishis, the slayer of Madhu went out... the Rishis, Narada and others vanished, for repairing to their respective places."

statements.claim: The Kauravas with all the kings followed him like the gods following Indra, but Sauri, of immeasurable soul, bestowed not a single thought on them and went out like a blazing fire mixed with smoke; Kritavarman's mail-clad ranks closed behind him.
statements.evidence: 5.131: "the Kauravas with all the kings followed him, like the gods following Indra. Sauri, however, of immeasurable soul, without bestowing a single thought on those that followed him, issued from the court, like a blazing fire mixed with smoke." (Ranks detail from Kritavarman's 5.130 arrayed troops.)

statements.claim: At the gate waited his charioteer Daruka with the great white car — tinkling bells, golden ornaments, cloud-rumbling wheels, white tiger-skins, and the steeds Saivya and her fellows; Kritavarman waited mounted on his own car.
statements.evidence: 5.131: "he beheld (at the gate his charioteer) Daruka waiting with his large white car, furnished with rows of tinkling bells, decked with golden ornaments... covered all over with white tiger-skins, and unto which were harnessed his steeds Saivya (and others). And there also appeared, mounted on his car, that favourite hero of Vrishnis, the mighty car-warrior Kritavarman."

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra pleaded that Krishna had seen the power he wielded over his sons and witnessed all; he had no sinful feelings toward the Pandavas and had made every endeavour for peace.
statements.evidence: 5.131 Dhritarashtra's speech quoted nearly verbatim ("O grinder of foes, thou hast seen... the power I wield over my sons!... I have no sinful feelings towards the Pandavas...").

statements.claim: Narrator notes the blind king had seen nothing with his own eyes and could only protest his good intentions.
statements.evidence: Dhritarashtra's blindness is canonical and he is absent from the list of those granted divine sight in 5.131; the gloss is grounded inference.

statements.claim: Krishna told Dhritarashtra, Drona, Bhishma, Kshattri Vidura, Vahlika and Kripa that they had witnessed how wicked Duryodhana left the court from anger and how Dhritarashtra described himself as powerless; with their permission he would return to Yudhishthira.
statements.evidence: 5.131: "The mighty-armed Janardana then addressed Dhritarashtra, Drona, grandsire Bhishma, Kshattri, Vahlika, and Kripa and said... With the permission of you all, I shall now go back to Yudhishthira."

statements.claim: Krishna saluted them, mounted his car and drove away from Hastinapura; the war was now only a matter of travel.
statements.evidence: 5.131: "Saluting them, that bull amongst men, Sauri then mounted his car and set out." Closing line is connective.

notes: Departure, Daruka's car, Dhritarashtra's plea and Krishna's farewell all track Ganguli 5.131 closely; no unsupported or contradicted claims.
